definition: Structured prediction or structured output learning is an umbrella term for supervised machine learning techniques that involves predicting structured objects, rather than discrete or real values.
details: Similar to commonly used supervised learning techniques, structured prediction models are typically trained by means of observed data in which the predicted value is compared to the ground truth, and this is used to adjust the model parameters. Due to the complexity of the model and the interrelations of predicted variables, the processes of model training and inference are often computationally infeasible, so approximate inference and learning methods are used.

explainer.lead: An umbrella term for supervised machine learning techniques that predict structured objects rather than discrete or real values. It matters because many real tasks—parses, tag sequences—have interdependent outputs.

tiers.eli5: Instead of guessing one number, the model builds a whole connected answer, like a family tree, where each part affects the others.
tiers.practitioner: Models are trained on observed sample-ground-truth pairs and tuned by comparing predictions to ground truth; the pitfall is that model complexity and output interrelations make exact training and inference often infeasible, so approximate methods are used.
tiers.paperLevel: Supervised learning that predicts structured objects rather than discrete or real values; because training and inference are often computationally infeasible, approximate inference and learning methods are used.

explainer.example: Translating a natural language sentence into a parse tree is a structured prediction problem whose output domain is the set of all possible parse trees.
